title: The reason for decision, in three sentences
summary: Learn what a ballot actually asks for, judge a live round between a parent and an AI, and deliver a reason for decision that names the clash, weighs it and says who won.
materials: the ballot page from week 1, and clean paper for a new one
a laptop with an AI assistant, driven by a grown-up who reads its case aloud
two grown-ups: one to debate and one to hold the timer

steps.title: What a reason for decision has to do
steps.body:
Last week you sat in the judge's chair for the first time and wrote a reason for decision. Today that reason gets a shape, and the shape is three sentences.

Sentence one names the clash. A clash is the one place the two sides actually met and disagreed about the same thing. Two speakers talking past each other is not a clash, however loud it gets. If you cannot point at the moment where one side answered the other, say so on the ballot, because that is a finding about the round and not a failure of yours.

Sentence two weighs it. Weighing is not summarising. It is saying why the winning answer to that clash mattered more than the losing one, in the round's own terms and not in yours. If both sides gave a reason and only one gave a reason plus something that happened in the world, that is a weighing you can write down.

Sentence three declares. Who won, and on what. Not who spoke better, not who was nicer, not who you agree with at the dinner table.

Three rules that make a ballot honest.

Judge the round, not the topic. If a side forgets its best argument, that argument does not exist today. Rescuing it is you debating, and you are not debating.

Your ballot is itself an argument. That means it can be wrong, and it means somebody is allowed to ask you to defend it. Today somebody will.

Write while you listen. A decision made from memory is a decision about whoever spoke last.

Now the round, and it is an odd one. One parent takes a side. The other side is argued by an AI assistant, prompted by a grown-up and read out loud. Here is the thing worth knowing before it starts: an assistant will write a fluent case for whichever side it is asked to take, and it will sound just as sure of itself either way. Fluent is not the same as true, and a confident voice is not evidence.

The motion: it is sometimes OK to lie.

The question of the week, and it belongs to this desert: is a mirage a lie? A mirage is real. Your eyes really see it and the light really bends. Nobody is lying to you. It is just not what it looks like. A speech can be a mirage too, and so can a program that compiles and runs and prints the wrong number. Looking true and being true are different things, and the judge's chair is where you get paid to tell them apart.

steps.title: Build the ballot before the round
steps.body:
Build the ballot before anybody speaks, because a ballot made afterwards is a memory test.

Take a clean page. Across the top: the motion, who is on which side, and the date. Down the page, one column for each speech in the order they will happen, wide enough to write in while somebody is talking.

At the bottom, box off three empty lines and label them clash, weighing, decision. Those three lines are the only ones you will read aloud.

While you listen, write what was said, not what you thought of it. Short is fine. When a claim later gets an answer, draw a line joining the two and write the same number at each end, so the pair can be found again in ten minutes.

When a side answers something the other side actually said, mark it. Those marks are where your clashes will come from, and there will usually be fewer than you expect.

One thing to watch for on purpose today, because the AI is in the room: mark any sentence that sounded true but named nothing real. A speech built entirely of those is a mirage, and it can still win if the other side never says so.
checklist: The ballot page exists before the first speech, with a column for every speech
The three lines at the bottom are labelled clash, weighing and decision, and they are empty
I wrote what was said rather than what I thought of it
Every place one side answered the other is marked on the page

steps.title: Judge it, then say why
steps.body:
Run the round properly. A grown-up holds the timer, both sides get the same time, and nobody coaches you.

You do not speak during the round. Not to agree, not to help, not to laugh at a good line. The chair is quiet.

When the last speech ends, take sixty seconds of silence and write the three sentences. Silence, not talking. The room waits.

Then read the reason for decision aloud, all three sentences, exactly as written. Do not add anything while you are reading it. If you find yourself adding, that is a sign a sentence was not finished, and that is a note for next time rather than a repair now.

Then the part that makes this real. Whoever lost gets one question, and you answer it. You are allowed to say that a sentence was wrong. A judge who can be moved by a good question is not a weak judge.

Last, one honest line for yourself, out loud on the recording: did you decide the round on what was said, or on what you already believed about lying before anyone opened their mouth?
checklist: I stayed quiet for the whole round, including the parts I wanted to join in on
I took the full sixty seconds of silence before writing the three sentences
The reason for decision names one clash, weighs it, and says who won and on what
The losing side asked me one question and I answered it out loud
I said whether I decided on the round or on what I already believed

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the reason for decision read aloud, all three sentences, then the losing side's question and your answer to it. Then, still recording, answer the question of the week in your own words: is a mirage a lie? Say what a mirage and a lie have in common and what makes them different kinds of thing.
